chief_complaint: progressive, symmetrical, chalk-white depigmented patches around eyes, mouth, and knuckles glowing under Wood lamp
hpi_details: 35F presenting with complete melanocyte loss patches glowing bright ivory-white under Wood's lamp responding to topical Tacrolimus 0.1% ointment and Narrowband UVB (NB-UVB) phototherapy.
ideas: She thinks the white patches are a chemical reaction to a harsh facial cleanser or a sun allergy that bleached her pigment.
concerns: She is worried that the white patches will spread across her entire face and hands, making people think she has a contagious skin disease and avoid shaking her hand.
expectations: She hopes to be prescribed a pigment-restoring cream or light treatment and get advice on medical cover-up makeup that won't rub off.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Vitiligo (generalized) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management of generalized Vitiligo combines topical anti-inflammatory agents (e.g., tacrolimus) with narrowband UVB phototherapy, adapted to disease extent and individual patient response.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: progressive, symmetrical, chalk-white depigmented patches around eyes, mouth, and knuckles glowing under Wood lamp

Key HPI features: 35F presenting with complete melanocyte loss patches glowing bright ivory-white under Wood's lamp responding to topical Tacrolimus 0.1% ointment and Narrowband UVB (NB-UVB) phototherapy.
Objective/Exam findings: Well-demarcated, symmetric, chalk-white depigmented macules and patches around the eyes, mouth, and knuckles that fluoresce bright ivory-white under Wood's lamp examination.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Vitiligo (generalized).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Tinea versicolor (scaly, not fully depigmented) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Rapid progression across large body surface area — may warrant more aggressive treatment.
management_principles: Confirm diagnosis clinically with Wood's lamp examination showing bright ivory-white fluorescence of depigmented patches.
Screen for associated autoimmune conditions, particularly thyroid disease.
Initiate topical calcineurin inhibitors (e.g., tacrolimus 0.1% ointment) for localized areas, especially the face.
Add narrowband UVB phototherapy for more extensive or refractory depigmentation, and refer to dermatology for ongoing management.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: An autoimmune destruction of melanocytes causing progressive, symmetric depigmented patches — classically around the eyes, mouth, and knuckles — confirmed by their bright ivory-white fluorescence under a Wood's lamp.
red_flags: Rapid progression across large body surface area — may warrant more aggressive treatment

must_ask.say: Are the patches symmetrical, appearing on both sides of your body in similar places?
Are the patches completely white, without any color at all?
Have the patches been spreading or getting larger?
Does anyone in your family have vitiligo or other autoimmune conditions, like thyroid disease?
How is this affecting you emotionally?

history.answer: I noticed completely white patches appearing and spreading around my eyes, mouth, and hands over the past several months.
They started about four months ago as small pale spots around my mouth and eyes, and over the past two months they have become completely chalk-white and spread to my knuckles.
They are located symmetrically around both eyes, around my lips, and over the knuckles of both hands.
They are stark chalk-white patches that are completely smooth, with clear borders and no flakes, scales, or redness.
No, they do not itch, burn, or hurt at all.
No, they stay there permanently once they appear and do not come and go or change through the day.
I have never had anything like this before in my life.
No, no fever, chills, fatigue, or body aches.
No, my lips, inside of my mouth, and private areas have no sores or blisters.
No, my skin is completely intact without peeling, blisters, or dark purple spots.
No, I have never had swelling of my face, tongue, or lips, and no difficulty breathing.
I have been on lisinopril for my blood pressure for over a year, and have not started any new prescription or over-the-counter medicines.
No, I haven't changed my face wash, cosmetics, lotion, or detergent, and no contact with chemicals or strange plants.
No one in my home has spots like this, and none of my coworkers have anything similar.
No, no insect bites, outdoor hiking, or visits to public baths or swimming pools.
No, I have never had eczema, asthma, or allergic rhinitis.
My joints feel fine without swelling or stiffness, and my nails look completely normal.
I haven't used any over-the-counter hydrocortisone or antifungal creams yet because I wanted to get an accurate evaluation first.
No, I have been in a monogamous relationship with my husband, and I have never had genital sores or infections.
I thought maybe an anti-aging facial peel I used bleached my skin, or that the sun somehow destroyed my pigment.
I'm really worried that it's going to spread all over my face and hands, and that clients at work will think I have something contagious and refuse to shake my hand.
I was hoping you could give me a cream to bring the color back and recommend a safe medical makeup so I can cover these spots today.
It has been emotionally exhausting; I feel so self-conscious talking to people and going to work with these stark white patches on my face.
I have high blood pressure and slightly elevated cholesterol, but no other medical problems.
No history of surgeries or hospital stays.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams once a day in the morning.
I have no known allergies to any medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I drink an occasional glass of wine, maybe once or twice a month at most.
I work as an office manager and live in an apartment with my husband.
No one has vitiligo, but my maternal aunt has an underactive thyroid condition called Hashimoto's disease.
My last menstrual period was two weeks ago, my cycles are regular every 28 days, and there is no possibility of pregnancy.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, pulse 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, temperature 36.6°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Well-appearing, alert, oriented, in no acute distress, but visibly distressed regarding facial appearance.

Symmetric, well-demarcated, chalk-white depigmented macules and patches around the bilateral eyes, perioral area, and dorsal knuckles, without erythema, induration, or scaling; fluoresces bright ivory-white under Wood lamp examination.
Normal visual acuity and extraocular movements; conjunctivae are clear without hyperemia or ulcerations, with normal periorbital depigmented skin.
Oral mucosa is moist and pink without depigmentation, erosions, or leukoplakia; tongue and posterior pharynx are normal.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, symmetric, smooth, non-tender, and moves freely with deglutition without palpable nodules.
No cervical, submandibular, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy palpable.
Fingernails and toenails are smooth without pitting, ridging, or onycholysis; interdigital skin is clear without scaling or burrows.
No depigmented patches, ulcers, or rashes on external genitalia.
